1.pericope_label: The poor cry out against mortgage, usury and the bondage of their children

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the complaint in its occasion: zealously as the rulers and richer members carried on the building after Nehemiah’s example, the work could not fail to be a heavy burden on the poorer classes, who found it difficult to maintain their families in expensive times and were still oppressed by wealthy usurers. They sort the outcry into three distinct complaints — those with no property who desired corn for their numerous families, those who had been obliged to mortgage fields, vineyards and houses to buy corn, and those who had borrowed upon their lands for the king’s tribute — and they correct the tense of the mortgage clause, since the participle shows that the pledging had already taken place and was still in force, so that the sense is not that they must pledge their fields to procure corn but that they have been obliged to pledge them and now ask for corn because of the dearth; what could be pledged was the crop, or such part of it as equalled the sum borrowed. On the appeal to common flesh they identify the brethren as the richer Jews who had lent upon pledges, and read the argument as this, that being of one flesh and blood with the rich the poor are of no worse condition than their wealthy fellow tribesmen, and yet their want is relieved only at the greatest interest where the law had directed that it be relieved freely. Ellicott marks what is new in the chapter, that Nehemiah’s other troubles had come from the enemies without and that he opens this account by laying emphasis on the hard treatment of Jews by Jews. He denies that a famine is meant at all: not any particular dearth, strictly speaking, but their present hunger, past mortgages having straitened their resources. He renders the tribute clause literally, that they had made their fields and vineyards answerable for the payment of the Persian tribute, having pledged the coming produce; and he calls the bondage of the children the climax of the cry, especially of the daughters, sold until the Jubile for money — children as precious to their parents as the rulers’ children were to them.

Clarke reaches back to the judicial dearth of the prophet’s time, when the heaven was stayed from dew and the earth from her fruit because the people ran each to his own house while the house of the Lord lay waste; its effects might still have been felt, but he thinks it more likely that a new dearth had come from the sheer number of people, for whose support the land brought into cultivation was not sufficient. He glosses the complaint as the plea of men whose families are larger than they can provide for, obliged to go into debt while their richer brethren take advantage of their necessitous situation; he explains the tribute as a tax paid to the Persian king in token of subjection, which though probably not heavy they were unable to pay; and he notes that the law permitted parents to sell their children in times of extreme necessity. Wesley turns the numerous offspring into a paradox, that it is in itself a blessing but to them was turned into a curse, and that they were forced to take up corn upon unreasonable terms. He offers three causes for the scarcity of his own: the multitude of people in and near Jerusalem, the work which wholly took them up and kept them from caring for their families, and the expectation of their enemies’ invasion, which hindered them from going abroad to fetch provision and the people round about from bringing it in. On the children he presses why the daughters are named, as evidence of great necessity, since they were more tender and weak and unfit for bond-service and more exposed to injuries than the sons, and he notes that the redemption the law allowed them was beyond their means.

Henry reads the passage as the tears of the oppressed, dropped before a governor whose office it was to deliver the poor and needy, and sums the causes in a phrase: hard times and hard hearts made the poor miserable. The times were hard, for there was a dearth of corn, probably for want of rain, with which God had chastised their neglect of his house and the non-payment of their church dues — and thus foolish sinful men bring God’s judgments upon themselves and then fret and complain of them. What made the scarcity more grievous was that the families which were most necessitous were the most numerous: here were the mouths, but where was the meat? Those who have great families and little substance must learn to live by faith in God’s providence, and those who have little families and great substance must make their abundance a supply for the wants of others. The taxes too were high, the king’s tribute being a remaining mark of their captivity and perhaps a poll-money, so that the more a man had to maintain the more he had to pay; and their families had come poor out of Babylon and been at great expense in building houses before these new burdens came. Then the persons they dealt with were hard: the lenders exacted twelve per cent, the hundredth part every month, forced them to mortgage lands and houses and took the profits for interest, that by degrees they might make themselves masters of all they had, and took their children for bond-servants. On that last point Henry gives the appeal its force, that our children are as their children, as dear to us as theirs are to them, free-born Israelites of the same holy nation, our flesh carrying the sacred seal of the covenant as well as our brethren’s.

Gill puts the claim of common standing plainly, that the complainants are of one nature, nation, stock and religion with their creditors, their children circumcised as theirs and entitled to the same privileges in church and state. He identifies the criers as those of the poorer sort, explains that the mortgaged lands had been made over and put into the lenders’ hands as pledges for money received, and guards the mention of their many children, since a numerous offspring was always reckoned a blessing among the Jews and was named here only to show how much food such families required.

6.pericope_label: Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, calls a great assembly, and binds them by oath to restore the pledges

schools.summary: Henry sets Nehemiah beside the other great reformer of the age: Ezra and Nehemiah were both of them wise, good and useful men, yet in cases not unlike there was a great deal of difference between their management, for when Ezra was told of the sin of the rulers he rent his clothes and wept and prayed and was hardly persuaded to attempt a reformation, while Nehemiah forced them to reform. He notes that the complaint reached the governor when his head and hands were as full as possible of the public business about the wall, yet perceiving it to be just he did not put it off; that he called the people together to be witnesses of what he said and to bear their testimony against the oppressions their rulers were guilty of; and that let no man imagine his dignity sets him above reproof.

Wesley repeats Henry’s comparison in brief, the one of a mild tender spirit and the other warm and eager, and adds the lesson that God’s work may be done and yet different methods taken in doing it, which is good reason why we should not arraign the management of others nor make our own the standard. He explains the purpose of the assembly, that it was called of rulers and people together, the greater part of whom were free from this guilt and therefore the more impartial judges, so that the offenders might be convinced and reformed, if not for fear of God or love of their brethren, then at least for the public shame and the cries of the poor. On the remedy he states the force of Nehemiah’s example, that he freely remits his own right and therefore they ought to do the same, since he lays no burden on them but what he is willing to bear a part of on his own shoulders; the hundredth part he takes for what was required every month for the use of their monies, according to the custom then used; the priests he takes as witnesses, so that the oath being made before men who acted in God’s name it might leave the deeper impression on their consciences; and the shaking of the lap he calls a form of swearing then in use. Clarke calls the usury expressly contrary to the law of God and doubly cruel at such a time, the people being just returned out of captivity and suffering from a dearth, and reports the view that this fell about a sabbatical year, when the land lay at rest and they were commanded to exact no debt. On the hundredth part he relays a sharp textual challenge, that the word nowhere means a hundredth part, that neither the Syriac nor the Greek nor the Arabic acknowledges one, and that remitting merely a hundredth to people so distressed would have answered no end at all, so that the phrase should rather be read as a part from the money. The shaking of the lap he calls a significant action frequent among the Hebrews, and sets beside it the Roman ambassadors who entered the senate of Carthage with the toga gathered in the bosom, declaring that they carried peace and war, and who then shook out the fold and said, we bring you war.

Ellicott credits the governor with self-command, since having recently arrived he had not known this state of things, and he corrects the description of the assembly, which was called not against them but concerning them. He locates the difficulty of the case exactly: the transgressors had violated the spirit rather than the letter of the law, so that the bare charge of exacting usury each of his brother failed in its object, and the appeal had to be shifted to the redemption of Jews from the heathen — Nehemiah and his friends had bought Jews back with money, while these men had caused Jews to be sold to Jews, an argument against which they could find nothing to answer though they might have replied had the letter of the law been urged. On the remedy he reads the governor’s plea as not for leaving off usury but for remitting the loans outright, and reckons the monthly charge at one per cent, twelve in the year, now given up for the future. He observes that a promise to restore had already been given, but that Nehemiah exacted an oath to give the proceeding legal validity, the priests’ presence lending it the highest religious sanction, and that the shaking of the lap imprecated on every covenant-breaker that he be emptied of all his possessions as the fold of the garment was emptied; and he adds the telling point that the iniquity thus stopped is not named in the later covenant, nor among the offences the governor found on his second return. Keil and Delitzsch find the usual rendering of the rebuke unworkable, since the words mean simply to lend a loan and Nehemiah can hardly reproach the nobles for lending when he and his servants had done the same; the injustice must lie rather in the emphatic position given to the word for the pledge. On the ninth verse they read the motive as public: we ought not, by harsh and unloving conduct toward our brethren, to give our enemies occasion to calumniate us.

Gill observes that the complaint raised both pity toward the poor and indignation at the rich who oppressed them, and that the governor consulted with himself what method was to be taken to redress such grievances. He notes the understatement in the words it is not good that ye do, by which much more is intended than is expressed. On the restitution he reports from Aben Ezra that this was the year of release, when debts were not to be exacted but forgiven, which would make the demand for an immediate restoration the more reasonable; and on the gesture he gives the same Roman parallel as Clarke, the ambassadors who had peace and war in the bosom of the garment to shake out as they chose.

They had violated the spirit rather than the letter of the law, so the bare charge of usury failed of its object

14.pericope_label: Nehemiah refuses the governor’s allowance for twelve years, keeps a daily table at his own charge, and prays to be remembered

schools.summary: Gill reconstructs the appointment, that Nehemiah was made governor by the king of Persia not when first sent into Judea but probably after he had finished the wall in fifty-two days, when he returned and gave the king an account of his success and of how things stood in those parts, and was then sent again in the character of a governor within the same year, so that the twentieth to the thirty-second year of the king makes twelve. He identifies the former governors as those between Nehemiah and Zerubbabel, Ezra having been no governor, and follows the Jewish chronology that Zerubbabel returned to Babylon and died there, his son succeeding him. He notes that the hundred and fifty at the table were entertained every day at Nehemiah’s own cost, which must have been considerable for such a number and of such rank; and he reads the closing prayer as expecting no recompense from the people but from the Lord, and from him not in the way of merit but of grace and good will, who does not forget what is done for his name’s sake.

Ellicott draws a compositional inference from the phrase about the twelve years, that the whole narrative thus far was written after the return from Jerusalem and on a review of the governorship, which is why Nehemiah calls himself their governor in the land of Judah and why nothing is said of the second appointment, which at the time of writing still lay in the future. He prices the old practice, taking the forty shekels as received over and above the bread and wine, which would amount to some four pounds daily from the entire people, and judges that the governors contrasted cannot include Zerubbabel but only some of his successors, such exactions being common among the satraps of the Persian princes; and he grounds Nehemiah’s stated motive in the law itself, where usury and rigour are interdicted with the express sanction, fear thy God. He renders the verb of the sixteenth verse as repaired rather than continued, that is, acted as superintendent, and observes that instead of taking advantage of the people’s poverty to acquire their land by mortgage he and his servants were absorbed in the common work. He calls the charge on the governor’s free hospitality heavy, and corrects the last clause of the eighteenth verse, which speaks not of bondage but of the service of building being heavy. Keil and Delitzsch identify the hundred and fifty as the heads of the different houses of Judah collectively, always guests at the table, together with such Jews as dwelt among the surrounding nations when they came to Jerusalem; they describe the daily provision as one ox, six choice and therefore fat sheep, and fowls, prepared at Nehemiah’s own expense, with a quantity of wine furnished every ten days which is not numbered but designated in general terms as very great; and they read the refusal as compassion, that notwithstanding this great expenditure he did not require the allowance due to him as governor, because the service of building the walls lay heavy upon his countrymen.

Wesley qualifies the span, that Nehemiah did not continue so long together at Jerusalem but governed it that long, by himself when present and in his absence by a deputy, the bread refused being that allowance which by the laws of God and nations and of the king of Persia the governors might require. Of the former governors he says they were not Ezra, who was no governor, nor Zerubbabel, but others between him and Nehemiah, whom he forbears to name; their servants ruled the people with rigour and cruelty, and that fault of the servants is charged upon their masters because they did not restrain them. He makes the fear of God the whole account of the difference: Nehemiah had an awe of God’s mercy and a fear of offending him, and those who truly fear God will not dare to do anything cruel or unjust, which is not only a powerful but an acceptable principle both of justice and charity. He notes that the governor oversaw and directed and encouraged the workmen at his own cost, and that his poor brethren’s necessities gave abundant opportunity of enriching himself with good bargains, which he refused; and that the rulers resorted to his table on all occasions, to give notice of the enemies’ designs or to receive his orders. Clarke describes what was declined, the governor’s table always supplied by the people with bread and wine and forty shekels a day besides for other expenses, and the people greatly oppressed by his servants and officers; through twelve years Nehemiah took no salary and ate none of their bread, nor were his servants permitted to exact anything, so that with such an example before them it was scandalous for the chiefs and priests and nobles to oppress an afflicted people. He reckons the daily provision food for more than two hundred men, wonders whether wine was drunk only every tenth day or merely laid in then, and sets beside the table of Nehemiah that of a modern eastern ruler who had twelve sheep daily with fish and fowls and soups and oranges and rice, his nobles dining with him, then the servants, then the poor taking what was left — the twelve sheep answering to six sheep and an ox, so that the two modes of living were nearly alike. To bear such expense he supposes Nehemiah had saved money while cup-bearer to the Persian king.

Henry insists on the purpose of the telling, that Nehemiah relates his practice not in pride or vain-glory nor to pass a compliment upon himself, but as an inducement both to his successors and to the inferior magistrates to be as tender as might be of the people’s ease. He notes that Nehemiah does not name his predecessors, because what he had to say of them was not to their honour, and in such a case it is good to spare names: the government allowed them forty shekels of silver, nearly five pounds and probably so much a day, but besides that they obliged the people to furnish bread and wine as perquisites of office and suffered their servants to squeeze the people. From which he draws two notes, that it is no new thing for men in public places to seek themselves more than the public welfare and to serve themselves by the public loss, and that masters must be accountable for the acts of fraud and injustice, violence and oppression, which they connive at in their servants. The fear of God restrained Nehemiah, and purely that, not the hope of praise from men nor any turn to be served by an interest in the people. Henry presses the test of outcome, that what a good hand the predecessors made of their place appeared by the estates they raised, while Nehemiah got nothing but the satisfaction of doing good, neither buying any land — say not then that he was a bad husband, but that he was a good governor, who aimed not to feather his own nest. He did the work of the governor but did not eat the bread of the governor, living on what he had got in the Persian court and his own estate in Judea, and the reason he gives is that the bondage was heavy upon the people: he might have pleaded that it wronged his successors not to demand his dues, but he could not find it in his heart to add to the burden of a people who already groaned.
